title: Substance and appearance (ST III.75)
hook: Thomas explains transubstantiation: the substance changes while appearances remain
carry: what it is, not how it looks

segments.voice: Yesterday, sacraments as instruments: God the craftsman, the sacrament his tool. Your line was God's tools.

At a family reunion, an old woman squints across the yard at a tall man with a gray beard and a cane. She doesn't recognize him. His hair is gone, he's far heavier than the skinny kid she used to babysit. Then he laughs, and she says his name. Everything about how he looks has changed. Who he is hasn't. Hold on to that, because Thomas Aquinas is about to turn it inside out. Today, the word he builds his account of the Eucharist on: substance.
screen: `EVERYTHING ABOUT HOW HE LOOKS CHANGED.` → `WHO HE IS DIDN'T.` → `NOW TURN IT INSIDE OUT.`

segments.voice: Thomas uses two words from philosophy. Substance is what a thing is. Accidents are the features it has: color, size, taste, weight, place. Usually the accidents change and the substance stays, like the man at the reunion. At Mass, Thomas says, it happens the other way around. At the Last Supper Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Take ye, and eat. This is my body." The Catholic Church takes those words literally. The whole substance of the bread is changed into the substance of Christ's body, and the wine into his blood, while the accidents remain: the color, taste and weight of bread and wine. The Church names this transubstantiation, first met on day one hundred fourteen: a change of substance. Thomas is careful about what it isn't. Christ's body doesn't travel down from heaven and push the bread aside. Nothing moves. It's a change in what is there, not where something goes. Why keep the look and taste of bread? People don't eat human flesh, and it would horrify them; so the gift comes as ordinary food. And it leaves room for faith. Are the senses fooled, then? No, he says. The senses judge appearances, and the appearances really are there. It's the mind, by faith, that knows what is underneath. In John, Jesus says: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." Christians understand this differently. Orthodox Christians also speak of a real change, without Thomas's terms; some Protestant churches understand the bread as a sign or memorial. Thomas's word asks you to look past how something looks to what it is.
screen: `SUBSTANCE: WHAT A THING IS.` · `THE SUBSTANCE CHANGES, THE LOOK REMAINS.` · `NOTHING MOVES.` · `THE SENSES JUDGE APPEARANCES.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BODY.`

segments.voice: Catholic churches keep the Eucharist in a tabernacle, and some leave their doors open; if you can stop in, sit near it for a while without saying much. If you can't, and you pray, turn your attention toward the nearest tabernacle you know. If you don't pray, look at one ordinary thing near you and ask what it is, beneath how it looks.
Substance. What a thing is, beneath the features you can see and touch. For Thomas, at Mass the substance changes while the appearances remain. Today's word.
Your line: what it is, not how it looks. People, too, are more than a glance can catch. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics genuflect toward the tabernacle where the Eucharist is reserved, receive Communion at Mass, and some parishes hold Eucharistic adoration, where people sit or kneel in prayer before the host.

chat.says: If it still tastes like bread, how can Catholics say it's Christ's body?
options: Thomas says the substance changes while the look and taste of bread remain.
Thomas says the bread's chemistry changes, though too slightly to detect.
Thomas says Christ's body comes down from heaven and pushes the bread aside.
chat.meaning: For Thomas, the bread's substance becomes Christ's body while its accidents, color, taste and weight, remain. The senses judge appearances truly; faith knows what's underneath.

accidents.meaning: a thing's features, like color, taste, size and place

transubstantiation.meaning: the change of the bread and wine's substance into Christ's body and blood

tabernacle.meaning: the box in a church where the Eucharist is kept

Orthodox Christians.meaning: Christians of the Eastern Orthodox churches

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: Christ's body is not there by local motion (III.75.2); the whole substance of bread converted into the whole substance of Christ's body (75.4); the accidents remain, for reasons including that it is horrible for people to eat human flesh, and for the merit of faith (75.5); the senses are not deceived since they judge accidents, and the intellect is kept from deception by faith (75.5 ad 2).
'Transubstantiation' is attributed to the Church (CCC 1376, Council of Trent); no date given.
Other churches: Orthodox speak of a real change without the scholastic terms; some Protestant churches understand the bread as a sign or memorial. Brief and unranked; confirm fairness.
Practice says Catholic churches keep the Eucharist in a tabernacle (reservation; CCC 1379); confirm wording.
Douay-Rheims wording and verse numbering to confirm: Matthew 26:26 and John 6:56 (Douay numbering).
Editor pass: 'at face value' changed to 'literally', since the lesson's point is that the face value (the look of bread) is not the substance.
